en: It was the time he entered a wondrous place,
The time he flew his falcon boldly,
The world forgotten from his mind,
The time the boy took his pleasure.
Making Akshumkar ready,
Semetey swung it out.
'Such joy and entertainment,
Such wonders I have seen today!'
Semetey reveled.
At the head of Batkaktuu,
Where thorns mingled with willows,
At the meeting of the thickets,
The boy was taking his pleasure.
Ysmayyl's kettledrum
Clanged when struck with a whip.
If a club struck the damned thing,
It boomed, shaking the earth.
The whip with dark handle
He grasped and swung round.
Into the middle of the kettledrum
Semetey struck.
Wild cries and hollow cheers
He sent ringing through the forest.
A blue hen pheasant, big as a little pail,
With iron spurs and a copper jess-plate,
Its golden wings two ells long,
Shot straight upward with a whir,
And fluttered eastward.
It seemed lit by moonlight.
Manas's orphaned son,
Enchanted by the hen pheasant,
Had his heart deeply stirred.
Was it Khizyr, rather than a pheasant?
To reach its mountain slope,
Was it an envoy passing between them?
Was it the eye of a saint?
Sary Khan and Semetey—
Was this the time to bring them together?
Unable to bear seeing the pheasant escape,
He turned Aktulpar's head.
Leaning sideways, Semetey
Cast Akshumkar forth.
The mighty champion, the dear lion,
Ah, the dear warrior, fierce as a cock,
Began with great fury.
He launched Akshumkar with such force
That Aktulpar beneath him
Nearly fell.
It stumbled and sank out of sight,
Tripped and righted itself,
Its fetlocks bending,
Turning round and staggering.
Aktulpar, a true racer,
Barely recovered its balance.
Akshumkar, released from the hand,
Rose and set its course,
As though it had not seen its quarry.
It circled and hovered,
Flying back, tilting away.
With iron talons and a copper jess-plate,
Two ells around,
Black-eyed, with blue-flecked legs,
It never spared what it was shown,
Never filled itself with a pail of meat,
Never ceased its eager fluttering,
Never filled itself with a platter of meat.
'You do not fold your wings and stoop,
Yet you let no goose fly from the lake;
You do not fold your tail and stoop—
Why has God struck you so?
Let alone a pheasant, Akshumkar,
You let no swan fly from the lake!
I shall untie your tether and free you,
And part with you in this forest.
If I do not speak my words of pardon,
Become a stranger to you here,
And turn back toward Bukhara!'
Then, saying this,
He shouted in fury,
Raising the battle cry, 'Temir!'
The whip with dark handle
He grasped and swung round.
Aktulpar beneath him
He struck upon the hock.
The white reins of tanned hide
He let loose without pulling them back.
The blood-drinker's offspring
Began pursuing the pheasant.
Wild cries and hollow cheers—
He spared not his voice,
And began pursuing the pheasant.
The pheasant in the sky, he on the ground,
He made a spectacle there.
Aktulpar, now in full condition,
Tore up the ground beneath it.
Clods as large as a great cauldron
Above the dear young lord's
Head went whirling.
Its hooves thundered upon the earth;
Its dark steel bit
Clattered within its throat.
Its mouth gaped like a ravenous maw;
White foam mixed with blood
Spattered its breast.
The earth split as it flashed across;
The winged racer Aktulpar
Ran straight on, drawing near.
Ysmayyl's Akshumkar,
Making a short flight and wheeling,
Shot ahead of an arrow.
Turning in a tight circle,
It darted toward the pheasant,
Just as it reached to seize its prey,
It plunged straight down and was checked.
Into a grass shelter, a half-sized dwelling,
The pheasant slipped uncaught and escaped.
Enthralled by the pheasant,
The orphan favored by Khizyr came on,
Beating the kettledrum,
And looking fiercely about.
To find the pheasant,
He gave no heed to his surroundings,
Sparing himself not at all,
Making his horse trample the forest.
Angry and tense,
At the falcon that had failed to catch it
He scolded harder than at a man:
'A harrier is a bird, and so are you.
If you were not a mere harrier,
If you caught the pheasant for me,
If I took it and slaughtered it lawfully,
If I fastened it to my saddle straps,
To my dear sister Kanykei,
That widow living as a fugitive,
If I went bearing it as a gift,
From my fierce brother-in-law Khan Manas,
The great wealth lying hidden—
If I asked for it and received it,
I could take my pleasure with a contented heart.
Damn your father's grave, Akshumkar!
I should have no complaint against you!
If you reached and struck the pheasant,
If you opened your eyes wide,
I could bind it up and fold it,
And secure it to my saddle straps.
For the great matron, my kinswoman by marriage,
If you caught the pheasant for me,
When I went to present it,
The enemy-surveying instrument left by Manas,
That precious telescope,
I could ask for it as a gift.
To that kinswoman by marriage, my sister,
When I would go bearing a gift,
You failed to reach the pheasant:
Has God struck you?
Meat from a yearling sheep's hock—
Yesterday, when I cut off its hock and gave it,
Did I throw you out of condition?
Or has God struck me?
Not pursuing hard, nor giving heed,
Has God struck you?
Spoiling you, not knowing your nature,
Has God struck me?'
Huffing and puffing in fury,
Semetey stood roaring.
At the falcon that had failed to catch it,
He spoke more harshly than at a man.
There beside the forest,
With four ropes upon his back,
A goatskin coat upon his body,
And leather trousers on his legs,
He had a path no dog would tread.
Moving his limbs like a human,
He had two arms upon his breast,
Brows like a dog lying down,
A head like a small cauldron,
And a single eye upon his forehead.
He has little of an envoy's courtesy.
Oozing scabs streamed from his bald crown.
He had an eye like a little bowl.
Then he saw Sary Taz.
He has little of an envoy's courtesy.
He saw a bald man like a devouring monster.
Blackened with soot from quenching charcoal,
Master of a great stretch of forest,
Perhaps his nights were not dark.
'A robber,' my khan father
Used to speak of such a one:
Perhaps this was one of those robbers.
Perhaps he spends his days lying in rushes,
Perhaps he is one of the monsters.
Forgetting the falcon, he wandered dazed,
Astonished at your elder Sary.
A great camel-necked sickle
Was fastened firmly at his waist.
He grasped it in both hands.
No person could approach,
No bear could withstand him.
The dark forest before him
He struck with the sickle,
Destroying it at the roots,
Shoving through it like a camel.
In the blink of an eye,
Before a word could be said,
He piled it up like a mountain.
All the bristling ground,
With club and staff in hand,
He beat down, leaving nothing.
Look at the wonder of that bald man!
With a Chinese fire-steel and striking stone,
He scraped and set an ember,
And kindled dry dung.
With a single 'Whoosh!' he blew.
A poker forty fathoms long in hand,
He stirred all around it,
Leaving no blackened brand,
Gathering it like a little herdsman's tent.
The charcoal came into view;
Blue embers as large as pails
Were separated with the poker.
That bald charcoal-burner's
Skill was plain to see.
Holding six pailfuls of water,
His dark handled bowl, big as an ox's head,
Into the bubbling dark spring
He plunged with a 'Thump!'
Making it spread and overflow,
He scooped up the water.
With a 'Gurgle!' he took a mouthful,
With a 'Puff!' he sprayed it.
In the blink of an eye,
He sprayed not once, but a thousand times.
The poker some forty fathoms long
He thrust into the charcoal.
Pawing like a blue bull,
He spread it all around.
Sixty camel-loads of charcoal
Lay there extinguished.
Seeing this feat of strength,
Semetey could not hold back:
'Greetings, peace be upon you,
Renowned elder Sary!'
He greeted him, but there was no reply.
Let alone a greeting, the bald man
Would not even look at him.
The bald man stood unmoved, unconcerned.
Semetey's greeting
He valued not a whit.
Courage and arrogance together
The Almighty God,
However wretched his life,
Had given that bald man without measure.
As the bald man stood ignoring him,
The boy burned and seethed like an ember,
His two eyes turned to fire.
